Date: 2027-03-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Cole (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (LumenPay Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (LumenPay Infra), Marta Lopez (LumenPay CTO), Diego Ramos (LumenPay SRE)
summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations tailored to LumenPay's payments workload. Discussed batching configs, expected hit-rates, cost tradeoffs, TTLs, and pilot plan. Customer wants a pilot with SOC2 and VPC constraints; action items: share cost model, run KV cache benchmark, provide prefix dataset, and schedule follow-up for private deployment details.
topics: Cost model: tokens saved vs latency impact
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we were gonna run through Redwood Optimize — batching, prefix and KV cache recommendations for the LumenPay workload. Quick roll call?
00:12 Aisha Patel: Hi, yes Aisha here. We really want to see the cost impact and how caching affects tail latency.
00:20 Tom Reynolds: Tom — infra. We're mainly concerned about VPC/network egress and also rate limits.
00:27 Marta Lopez: Marta — CTO. High level: pilot in Q2, must be SOC2-aligned.
00:33 Jordan Kim: Great. Priya and Evan from our SE team will run the technical bits.
00:38 Priya Nair: Hi all. Short agenda: 1) batching types and configs, 2) prefix vs KV cache, 3) cost model with examples, 4) pilot asks.
00:47 Diego Ramos: quick q: when you say prefix cache is that the prefix-only or a full KV-store?
00:52 Priya Nair: Good question — prefix cache is a short prefixes cache we use for common opening tokens, KV cache is the full key-value KV cache for long-running contexts — sometimes called the 'kv-cache' or 'kv cash' in transcripts, haha. Both help in different ways.
01:05 Priya Nair: So starting with batching: Redwood supports dynamic batching where requests are coalesced in the runtime based on a batching window, or you can set micro-batch sizes on the client side. For latency-sensitive traffic we usually recommend smaller windows, e.g., 10-30ms. For high throughput background jobs you can push to 50-150ms.
01:28 Aisha Patel: Our average sequence length is around 220 tokens for parsed receipts but conversational flows go up to 1,100 occasionally.
01:36 Priya Nair: Okay that's useful; for tails like 1,100 we typically fall back to model variants or shard the KV. Our cost model will show how much batching helps at 220 vs 1,100.
01:48 Jordan Kim: Quick note on models: if you want, we can route higher seq-length calls to a cheaper quantized variant during bursts — that was part of the routing discussion.
01:57 Tom Reynolds: Any implications for the KV cache size on GPU memory? We worry about OOM on peaks.
02:05 Evan Cole: Yes — KV cache is stored per-session (or per-actor) in GPU memory; we do chunking and eviction policies. For your workload with 1,100 token sessions we recommend a per-session cap and a shared LRU for cold sessions.
02:20 Priya Nair: Also important: hit-rate. If your prefix distribution is Zipf-like (few prefixes cover many queries) prefix cache gives big wins with minimal memory. The KV cache helps more for long context reuse.
02:34 Aisha Patel: Our user prompts have a lot of repeated legal intro lines — so prefix hit-rate should be high.
02:40 Priya Nair: Perfect — that suggests prefix caching will give high token savings. Let's run some back-of-the-envelope numbers.
02:46 Priya Nair: Example: assume prefix hit-rate 40% on token positions 0-50, batching improves tokens/sec via kernel amortization. If average request tokens generated is 220 and prefix 30 tokens saved on 40% of requests, that's 12 saved tokens per request on average.
03:05 Jordan Kim: And token cost differentials, right — if hosted model costs $X per 1k tokens, we can map saved tokens to $ saved per 1k requests. We'll send a spreadsheet.
03:16 Aisha Patel: Can you explain TTLs — how long do cached entries live, and what's the invalidation story?
03:22 Priya Nair: TTLs are configurable. For prefix cache we usually do short TTLs (minutes to hours) depending on variability. For KV cache session-based; typical TTL is the session lifetime. Invalidate on prompt changes or model updates.
03:35 Tom Reynolds: Security question: is KV data encrypted at rest? KMS? audit logs?
03:40 Jordan Kim: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we support KMS/HSM integrations and full audit logs. We'll attach our SOC2 and KMS integration doc. For hosted we encrypt in transit and at rest and can enable customer-managed keys for enterprise.
03:51 Marta Lopez: We need SSO/SAML and RBAC too — we want control over access.
03:56 Jordan Kim: Yep — SAML SSO, SCIM and role-based access are supported. We'll include config pointers.
04:03 Priya Nair: Back to performance: Let's walk a sample cost model. If baseline without caching is 1.0x cost, a 12-token average saving on a 220-token response is ~5.5% token reduction. But batching improvements can give 10-30% CPU/GPU efficiency improvements depending on sequence shape and kernel amortization. Together you can see 15-35% unit cost reduction.
04:27 Aisha Patel: That's helpful. Do you have benchmark numbers from similar payments customers?
04:31 Priya Nair: We do — for a consumer-payments pattern with similar prefix repetition we saw ~28% cost reduction after prefix caching + tuned batching. We'll share an anonymized case study.
04:40 Diego Ramos: What about latency p50/p95 — the caching sometimes adds lookup overhead, right?
04:45 Evan Cole: Lookup is a tiny mem-read in most cases; caching reduces decoder steps by removing repeated prefix tokens. The p95 improvements depend on batching policy; if you increase batching window you can hurt p95. So we tune per-route.
04:58 Priya Nair: Example: for a telco-like low-latency route we run smaller windows and aggressive prefix caching. For background ingestion we allow larger batch windows.
05:09 Aisha Patel: How do you estimate hit-rate before we run a pilot?
05:13 Priya Nair: We ask for a sample of prompts — ideally de-identified. You provided a small prefix set earlier; if you can provide a 100k sample we can run a quick offline hit-rate sim and give a predicted savings number.
05:24 Aisha Patel: We can do that, yes. We'll scrub PII.
05:28 Jordan Kim: Great — that'll let us populate the cost model spreadsheet.
05:33 Tom Reynolds: For the pilot — will network egress increase cost? We have strict egress limits.
05:38 Jordan Kim: For hosted calls there's standard egress; for Dedicated/Private we can keep traffic within your VPC and avoid extra egress charges. We'll outline the VPC topology.
05:48 Marta Lopez: How about fallback behavior if your dedicated capacity is saturated?
05:52 Priya Nair: We support smart routing policies — we can route to a lower-cost hosted pool or to a smaller quantized model variant during spikes. That keeps the app online with graceful degradation.
06:02 Diego Ramos: One more infra: KV cache persistence — is it per-GPU or can it be sharded across nodes?
06:08 Evan Cole: We can shard KV storage across nodes; sessions are pinned but part of the cache can be eviction-friendly and recomputed from prefix cache if needed. It's part of how we avoid OOMs.
06:19 Aisha Patel: Example numbers? If we do a 100k req/day pilot what's the expected latency and cost?
06:25 Priya Nair: Quick estimate — baseline avg latency 120-180ms for model X; with tuned batching we might see 100-140ms and a cost delta of ~20% lower tokens and 15-25% cheaper GPU time, depending on hit-rate. We'll produce a per-1k-request estimate in the spreadsheet.
06:42 Jordan Kim: I'll put an example line: 1k requests, avg 220 tokens, prefix hit-rate 40% => token units saved: 12k tokens per 1k requests. At $X per 1k tokens that's $Y saved.
06:58 Aisha Patel: Ok please call out assumptions in the spreadsheet.
07:02 Jordan Kim: Will do.
07:05 Tom Reynolds: On observability — can we see per-route token breakdowns and cache hit metrics?
07:10 Priya Nair: Yes — Redwood Console has per-route dashboards with token-level cost breakdown, cache hit-rate, and trace hooks. We can create a sample dashboard for your pilot routes.
07:21 Marta Lopez: About pilot success criteria: we care about 1) <150ms p50, 2) <300ms p95, 3) 20% cost reduction vs current endpoint. Can you commit to measuring those?
07:33 Jordan Kim: Yep — we'll create an SLA-like pilot metric doc and instrument the routes.
07:38 Diego Ramos: Any friction to integrating our KMS?
07:41 Jordan Kim: For Dedicated/Private it's straightforward — we support AWS KMS and bring-your-own-key. We'll include step-by-step.
07:48 Priya Nair: Drill into technical tuning: batching windows, tokenization alignment, and quantization. For tokenization alignment, we sometimes group requests so tokens line up and batching is more efficient — small engineering effort on the client side.
08:03 Aisha Patel: Who owns client-side changes? We prefer minimal changes.
08:07 Jordan Kim: We can handle client SDK patches as part of the pilot, or provide code snippets. Typically it’s a 1-2 day dev effort to adopt micro-batching wrapper.
08:16 Tom Reynolds: For pilot duration and scale?
08:19 Jordan Kim: Recommend 2-4 weeks at production-ish traffic — e.g., 100k requests/day — to capture steady state. Shorter smoke tests are possible but less reliable for hit-rate.
08:30 Aisha Patel: Sounds fine. We'll aim for mid-April pilot start but need SOC2 docs first.
08:36 Jordan Kim: We'll send SOC2 and KMS docs by tomorrow. Action items we'll recap at the end.
08:43 Priya Nair: Any last technical Qs?
08:46 Marta Lopez: One: do you support per-customer custom quantization? Like 4-bit for heavy users?
08:51 Evan Cole: We support multiple quantization profiles and can pin a route to a specific quantized variant. There's a tradeoff in quality but for most completions it’s negligible.
08:59 Aisha Patel: Ok, that's all on my side.
09:02 Jordan Kim: Quick recap of next steps: Jordan to share spreadsheet and SOC2 docs, Priya to run KV cache bench, customer to send prefix sample and confirm VPC/egr constraints. We'll set follow-up for deep-dive on private deployment.
09:17 Marta Lopez: Thanks everyone.
09:19 Jordan Kim: Thanks, bye.
09:22 (call ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings: 'KV cash' appears for 'KV cache' in places, and some acronyms like SSO/SAML are transcribed as SSO SAML without punctuation. Timestamps approximate; the call actually ran ~46 minutes; above transcript includes the first 9-ish minutes captured with representative excerpts and paraphrases.
